You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer rules from demos.

# Continual-ARC reasoning

Use this skill for ARC-style tasks in a recurring puzzle stream, especially when the interaction allows requesting demonstrations and submission attempts are costly.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the interaction contract.** Preserve the required response format exactly; choose one action per turn. Treat demo requests and wrong submissions as costly, and do not spend either without a reason.
2. **Inspect demonstrations comparatively.** Track dimensions, background, marker/object colors, and every changed cell. Form a compact rule that explains all examples, rather than fitting only the most visually salient region.
3. **Separate evidence from hypothesis.** Prefer a rule that predicts multiple independent changes in each demo. If ambiguity remains and the cost is justified, request another demo before submitting.
4. **Apply the rule mechanically.** Use a small script or structured representation for large grids when useful. Preserve original marker cells and untouched background; do not rely on manual transcription for a long output.
5. **Validate before submitting.** Check row count, column count, allowed values, unchanged source cells where appropriate, and consistency of every changed cell with the inferred transformation. Re-read the exact test input when constructing the result.
6. **Submit only the requested artifact.** In strict ARC interaction formats, avoid explanatory text if the protocol calls for a single action object.

## Common geometric transformation: connect aligned markers

A recurring pattern is a sparse set of same-color marker cells on a uniform background. Demonstrations may show a third color filling the straight gaps between consecutive markers that share a row or column. See [references/aligned-marker-lines.md](references/aligned-marker-lines.md) for how to infer and implement this rule, including boundary and overlap checks.

### Validated recurrence: task-83eba677 horizontal gap fill

For task-83eba677, fill only the cells strictly between consecutive same-color markers in each row with color 2. Do not fill vertical alignments, even when markers share a column. Preserve marker cells and all unrelated background cells. A further accepted 13×17 test had background 8, marker 0, with multiple horizontal chains; precisely the cells between consecutive 0s in each row became 2, while vertical alignments and isolated markers were left unchanged. This holds for single-cell gaps as well as longer gaps: a newly accepted 18×24 test (background 4, markers 8) had horizontal marker runs spanning gaps of several cells; every intervening cell between consecutive 8s in a row became 2, with other cells unchanged. Prior fresh cases also confirmed background 6/marker 1 and background 3/marker 5, plus an accepted 17×13 background 1/marker 8 case (29 changed cells). The 5×6 case had pairs at row 2 columns 0/2 and row 4 columns 1/3 (0-based), yielding 2 at the intervening cells only. Infer fill color 2, not from background or marker color.

## Full-line recoloring (validated task-5ebf4030)

For task-5ebf4030, identify complete horizontal rows and vertical columns consisting entirely of the same non-background color (color 7 in the demo; color 3 and 6 in fresh tests). Recolor every cell of each such full line to 2. Preserve all other cells, including occurrences of the line color outside complete lines. A newly solved 6×27 test had background 1 and line color 6; the only full row was row 2 (0-based), and full columns were 11, 19, and 25. Recolor those four lines to 2 while retaining partial 6s elsewhere. The demo had a full vertical line and a full horizontal line; the fresh 28x9 test had two full vertical lines and two full horizontal lines. This criterion reproduced the demo output and was accepted on fresh tests with two full vertical and two full horizontal lines (28x9), and on a 20x10 test with complete horizontal rows 3, 4, 5, 8, 10 and complete vertical column 4 (0-based). The latter confirms that full lines are recognized by the uniform line color even when the surrounding grid is a mixed 8/6 field; all complete 6-lines become 2. A second fresh 21x25 test used color 5, with complete rows 4 and 13 (0-based) and complete columns 10, 12, 17, and 22; all these lines became 2 while all other cells were preserved. Another accepted 19×24 recurrence had background 5 and line color 7, with full rows 7, 14, and 16 and full columns 12 and 17 (zero-based); precisely these lines were recolored to 2, including their intersections, while all partial 7s were preserved. Another accepted 9×7 test used background 6 and line color 0: full rows 4 and 8 and full column 5 (zero-based) were recolored to 2; all other 0s, including partial occurrences, were preserved. This confirms the uniform-line rule applies when the line color is zero. A further accepted 5×22 case had background 4 and line color 3; full row 4 and full columns 6 and 15 alone were recolored to 2, with all partial 3s preserved. Apply only to full single-color lines, not merely dense or partial alignments.

## Validated motif-stamping substrate

For task-868ab99b, extract the foreground mask of the uniquely colored seed motif and stamp that mask in its seed color at every translation where **all occupied mask offsets overlay 0-cells**. The dominant field color can vary (e.g. 8 or 9) and is not the placement substrate; requiring mask offsets to match the dominant color is wrong. Ignore mask bounding-box cells that are not foreground, and preserve all cells outside the stamped mask. This rule reproduced the provided demos and a fresh test.

For task-7a5e2600, do not assume a fixed mask across instances. Extract the foreground mask from that instance's seed and stamp it in the seed color at every translation where all occupied offsets overlay cells of color 0; replace only those zero cells and preserve every other cell. Validated examples show the mask varies: demo 1 had a 7-cell 4×3 mask with offsets {(0,1),(1,0),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1),(3,1),(3,2)}; demo 2 and the accepted fresh test had a 9-cell 4×4 mask with offsets {(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1)}. In both variants, requiring only occupied mask offsets to overlay zeros reproduced the demonstrated / accepted transformations; do not require the whole bounding box to be zero.

Do not infer motif substrate rules universally; for other tasks, determine the mask, seed color, and placement substrate from demonstrations.

### Validated recurrence: task-7a5e2600 motif stamping

Do not assume a fixed mask across instances: extract the seed foreground mask anew from each instance. Stamp that mask in the seed color at every translation where all occupied offsets overlay cells of color 0; replace only those zero cells and preserve all other cells, including the seed and nonzero field. Two validated mask variants: demo 1 used a 7-cell 4×3 mask with offsets `{(0,1),(1,0),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1),(3,1),(3,2)}`; demo 2 and the accepted fresh test used a 9-cell 4×4 mask with offsets `{(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1)}`. For each, requiring only the occupied offsets to overlay zeros reproduced the demonstrated / accepted transformation. Do not require the whole bounding box to be zero.

## Periodic stripe completion (validated task-eca8fe17)

For task-eca8fe17, demos show a sparse periodic color field encoded by colored full stripes/lines. Infer the repeating cycle and orientation from the line markers, then tile that cycle across the whole grid, replacing zeros as well as preserving the encoded colors. Examples: horizontal stripes can encode a row-period cycle (period 6 in the 8x8 demo; period 7 in the 11x11 demo), while parallel slope-−1 diagonal stripes encode phases of a cycle by `row+column mod period` (period 4 in the 28x28 demo). For fresh tests, do not assume one orientation or period; identify line direction and phase-color mapping from the current input/demos. Validated mappings include: a 28×28 parallel slope−1 diagonal field with period 4 encoded by `(r+c) mod 4`, phases 0→4, 1→2, 2→1; and task-eca8fe17 fresh tests where `(r+c) mod 3` mapped phases 0→4, 1→2, 2→1. A separate 8×8 test had parallel slope+1 diagonal markers, period 5 encoded by `(r−c) mod 5`, with phases 0→1, 1→9, 2→6, 3→5, 4→3; fill every cell using this cycle while preserving the encoded marker colors. A successful 23×23 test had a period-3 slope+1 diagonal field, with `c−r mod 3 = 0,1,2` mapped to colors `6,6,2` respectively (equivalently, color 2 at `c−r ≡ 2 mod 3`, color 6 elsewhere); marker 2s fixed that phase and overlapping 6 diagonal bands confirmed the remaining phase assignments. Fill every cell with the periodic field, not merely extending gaps.

### Confirmed task-eca8fe17 horizontal full-row cycle fresh test
A 7×7 test had each row uniform, with row colors `[0,9,3,6,9,8,0]`. Correct output row colors were `[8,9,3,6,9,8,9]`, i.e. repeat the six-row cycle `[8,9,3,6,9,8]` from row 0. The colored rows at indices 1–5 validated this period and phase; zeros at rows 0 and 6 were unknown slots, not cycle colors. Accepted. Infer the smallest supported periodic sequence and fill zero rows; preserve the demonstrated cycle colors.

## Noisy rectangular-field reconstruction (validated task-7a9d058a)

The grid is a patchwork of uniform rectangular color regions on a uniform background, corrupted by sparse arbitrary noise symbols. Recover each rectangle's exact bounds from repeated full spans and intact runs, then recolor every cell inside it (including noise/outliers) to that region's color. Set every non-rectangle cell to the background, including isolated colored speckles. Do not treat one digit as globally noisy, and do not assume 0 means empty: 0 can be the legitimate color of an entire region. Demos validate this: one has background 9, a 0 rectangle at rows 1–7/cols 4–9, a 3 rectangle at rows 12–15/cols 8–10, and a 0 rectangle at rows 14–20/cols 3–4, with many arbitrary intrusions and exterior speckles; another has background 3, a 6 rectangle at rows 2–5/cols 3–5 and 8 rectangles at rows 0–3/cols 8–9 and rows 6–7/cols 7–10, with stray values removed/restored. Fresh accepted 20×29 test (background 6) has rectangles: color 2 at (r0–3,c0–1), (r2–8,c6–8), (r5–11,c1–2), (r6–8,c10–14), (r6–7,c27–28), (r13–19,c13–19), (r15–19,c3–4); color 4 at (r0–4,c12–14), (r0–3,c16–21), (r0–2,c23–26), (r15–17,c7–11), (r17–18,c21–24); color 5 at (r5–11,c16–22), (r9–13,c24–28), (r9–11,c5–7), and (r16–17,c26–28). Coordinates are zero-based, endpoints inclusive. This accepted test corrected the rejected candidate by extending the upper 4 field to row 3 and the far-right 5 field through row 13; it also established a separate 5 rectangle at rows 9–11, cols 5–7. Carefully audit every outer boundary; an adjacent singleton must not extend a region unless the rectangle's repeated runs establish it. Validate every inferred rectangle against all demos, ensure rectangles do not overlap, check that all reliable object-color cells are accounted for, and clear every exterior anomaly to the background before submission.

## Comparing aligned panels with sparse zero-cells

When a divider separates aligned panels, infer the cellwise predicate from the demos rather than assuming that each panel's modal color defines its semantic background. In the validated task-192705d2 pattern, output a 2 where both corresponding input cells are nonzero, and 0 otherwise. The panels can have different dominant colors (for example, 5 on one side and 0 on the other; or 8 and 6 on a fresh test), while literal 0 is the empty-cell value. Thus implement `left_cell != 0 and right_cell != 0`; do not implement “both are non-background relative to each panel’s mode,” which incorrectly selects shared zeros in a 8/6 test. This was confirmed by a rejected shared-zero candidate followed by a correct nonzero-overlap submission. A fresh 4×9 recurrence had a single divider column (color 1) between two 4×4 panels; exclude the divider and produce a 4×4 mask by the same nonzero-overlap predicate. A further accepted 7×27 test used a full horizontal divider row (color 6) between 3×27 panels (dominant colors 1 and 9); exclude the divider and output the 3×27 nonzero-overlap mask. This confirms the same predicate applies to horizontal as well as vertical panel splits. Another accepted 10×15 recurrence had a full vertical color-8 divider at column 7, with 10×7 panels; left cells were sparse 6s and right cells sparse 4s. The accepted 10×7 output placed 2 exactly at nonzero overlaps: zero-based (r4,c5), (r5,c6), and (r7,c6), with all other cells 0. This reinforces that different nonzero colors count, and do not align the right panel including the divider. Always replay the predicate against the demo outputs and exact fresh input before submitting.

## Validated task-65d930f4 three-band mirror tiling

For task-65d930f4, expand an H×W input to 3H×2W. Each output row is the input row mirrored left-to-right, concatenated with the original row. Stack three vertical bands: input rows bottom-to-top, then top-to-bottom, then bottom-to-top. Equivalently, output row source indices are `H-1..0`, `0..H-1`, `H-1..0`. Preserve all source cell values; this is a geometric reflection/tiling rule, not recoloring. Confirmed on the 5×4 demo (15×8 output), a fresh 3×9 test (9×18 output), and a fresh 1×12 test (3×24 output). For the 1×12 input `[5,0,1,3,4,3,7,6,9,3,2,8]`, each of the three output rows was `[8,2,3,9,6,7,3,4,3,1,0,5,5,0,1,3,4,3,7,6,9,3,2,8]`; accepted.

## Validated task-0cc95332 two-color normalization

For task-0cc95332, every input cell is one of two colors: the distinguished value 5 and one instance-specific alternate color. Recolor all 5 cells to that alternate color, and recolor every alternate-color cell to 0. The alternate color varies by instance; do not assume it is a fixed value. Direct demo evidence: demo 1 used `{5,2}` and mapped `5→2, 2→0`; demo 2 used `{5,8}` and mapped `5→8, 8→0`. The accepted fresh 20×16 test used `{5,6}` and mapped `5→6, 6→0`. The first rejected attempt on that test mapped `5→2, 6→0`, showing that the destination is the other input color, not fixed 2. The next rejected attempt inverted the mapping (`5→0, 6→2`). In future instances identify the pair of colors and apply the mapping exactly; preserve dimensions.

## Pitfalls

- A marker may belong to both a horizontal and a vertical segment; preserve the marker color at intersections.
- Fill only the gap between consecutive markers in a row or column unless demos establish extrapolation or another endpoint rule.
- A visually plausible line rule is still a hypothesis until all demo changes are explained. In particular, inspect apparent extra fills as possible perpendicular segments before concluding they are unexplained.
- Keep coordinates and row/column indexing explicit to avoid one-cell shifts.

# Continual-ARC task-5be993db: unresolved evidence and recurrence notes

## Status

Simple clean partial horizontal bars have now been accepted on two fresh recurrences: (1) in a 16×16 grid, row 12 had color 2 at cols 0–10 and background 7 at cols 11–15; exactly that suffix became 1; (2) in the current 22×26 grid, row 10 had color 6 at cols 0–20 and 0 at cols 21–25; exactly cols 21–25 became 1, while the full-width color-6 row 1 and all other rows remained unchanged. This further supports changing the strictly trailing background suffix of an incomplete clean horizontal bar to 1, while preserving full-width bars. Do not assume it resolves the more complex selective-pattern variants: multiple suffix-fill variants were rejected on a different test. Treat patterned/intermittent contexts as unresolved and replay all available demos before generalizing.

## Demonstrated facts (current 29x24 test instance)

Every changed cell in the 8 demonstrations changed from the field/background color to 1; dimensions and all other cells were preserved. Changed coordinates below are zero-based row, column:

1. Demo 1 (25x17): row 7, col 16; row 8, col 16; row 9, col 16.
2. Demo 2 (10x18): row 8, col 17 (input value 4, with the preceding row segment all 2).
3. Demo 3 (10x10): row 6, cols 3–9 (three 7s at cols 0–2, then background to the right edge).
4. Demo 4 (20x23): rows 15–16, cols 21–22 (a 2x2 right-edge patch).
5. Demo 5 (27x17): rows 21, 23, 24, and 25, cols 13–16 (four separated 1x4 patches).
6. Demo 6 (27x26): row 22, cols 9–25 (a long suffix after nine 7s).
7. Demo 7 (10x10): row 8, cols 8–9 (a 1x2 right-edge patch).
8. Demo 8 (27x10): rows 4 and 6, cols 8–9 (two 1x2 right-edge patches).

Several positive examples have a horizontal foreground arrangement ending before a background-colored region at the right edge. There are also repeated/related motifs and rows that look similar but remain unchanged. Selection/context is not resolved by suffix geometry alone. Inspect the complete demos in the archived session rather than relying only on this summary.

## Important counter-evidence / rejected variants

A separate earlier instance of this task was accepted with a simple-looking transformation: on an 18x25 grid (background 3, marker 4), row 6 had a 4-run in cols 0–13 and the background tail cols 14–24 became 1; another full-width row of 4s was unchanged. This establishes that tail recoloring occurs in at least one case, **not** that all such tails should be recolored.

In the later 29x24 instance (background 5, foreground 7), eight demos were exhausted and all eight submissions were rejected. Rejected candidate families included:
- recolor the tail after the rightmost 7 in each active row;
- recolor tails after the longest/solid 7 run;
- recolor lower rows 21–22 after the long bar, in several tail widths;
- recolor only row 6's final background cell, alone or combined with lower tails.

The final test's active rows were 5, 6, 21, and 22 (zero-based):
- r5: `5 5 7 5 5` then a 7-run through the right edge;
- r6: 7 pattern at c0–3, c5–14 solid 7s, then alternating 7/5 through c23;
- r21: left motif, c7–17 are 7s, c18–23 are 5s;
- r22: left motif, c7–16 are 7s, c17–23 are 5s.
The candidates that recolored these lower tails and/or r6's final cell were rejected. Thus do not repeat them or infer that “longest run”, “row reaches edge”, or “same lower pair” alone is sufficient.

## Additional unresolved recurrence: 12x27 patterned test

A separate instance (background 8, foreground 5) had two active rows at r1-r2 and a patterned 2-row motif at r9-r10. Eight submissions were all rejected. Do not infer a fresh rule from the simple suffix reference without discriminating the patterned context. In particular, rejected full-grid candidates included: (a) replacing every trailing 8 after the rightmost 5 in each active row (r1 c15–26, r2 c17–26, r9 c25–26); (b) replacing alternating even-position 8s in the upper tails; (c) replacing all of r1's tail and extending a period-3 motif in r2; and (d) transferring foreground locations from lower rows 9–10 into corresponding 8-cells of upper rows 1–2. A candidate altering only parts of the lower patterned rows was also rejected, as was a malformed-grid candidate. Feedback was only whole-grid incorrect, so none of these rejections localizes the bad edit. At the end, 8/8 attempts and 8/8 demos were exhausted; no correct output was established. The exact trigger for selective suffix edits in this morphology remains unresolved. Preserve this as negative evidence; do not choose a near-duplicate candidate merely by changing the tail boundary.

## Additional accepted recurrence: task-5be993db 22×25 simple bar suffix

A fresh test was solved with 0 wrong attempts and no demos. Input was 22×25, background 0, with full-width color-9 row at zero-based row 8 and an incomplete color-9 horizontal bar at row 16, columns 0–19, followed by background 0 at columns 20–24. The accepted output changed exactly those five trailing background cells (row 16, cols 20–24) to 1. The full-width color-9 row and all other cells remained unchanged. This confirms the simple partial-horizontal-bar suffix-to-edge behavior on another background/bar color pair. Still do not generalize to complex/patterned variants: those remain unresolved and prior attempted extensions were rejected.

## Recommended approach on recurrence

1. Retrieve the full prior transcript and all 8 pairs, and make exact input/output diffs. Note repeated motif alignment, local row/column context, dimensions, and both positive and negative examples.
2. State a complete candidate rule that explains *which* row segments are selected, why similar-looking unchanged cells are excluded, and why the output color is 1. Reproduce the candidate on every demo before applying it to a test.
3. Use any available demo requests to discriminate named hypotheses; do not exhaust them without recording each pair's implications.
4. Mechanically construct and validate output dimensions and the precise changed-cell set. Under the puzzle protocol, respond with exactly one action JSON.

This note is deliberately labeled unresolved; no rule from the failed patterned-tail instances should be promoted to confirmed evidence.

## Later recurrence: task-5be993db 23×28 selective right-tail completion (accepted)

A fresh 23×28 test (background 5, marker 4) was solved correctly with no wrong submissions after three demo requests. The test output changed only the trailing background cells in rows 8–11 (zero-based), columns 25–27, to color 1. Every other cell remained unchanged. Rows 16–19 had a solid 4 block through the right edge and were unchanged; all other rows were background-only.
